# Exodus 28:23–43 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Verses 23–28: The Fastening of the Breastpiece to the Ephod

**v. 23 — Two gold rings on the two upper corners of the breastpiece.**

These two rings are placed on the two upper corners ("ends") of the breastpiece. The gold chains (described earlier in v. 14) are to be passed through them and then united with the "ouches" (settings) on the shoulder-pieces of the ephod. — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm ; Pulpit, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/28-23.htm

Gill notes these rings were on the upper part of the breastpiece, toward the two shoulder-pieces of the ephod, at the right and left upper corners. — Gill, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-28.html

**v. 24 — Fasten the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece.**

The two braided chains of pure gold are put through the two rings on the upper ends of the breastpiece. Keil & Delitzsch note that these chains, called "cords" or "strings" here, are the same as those first mentioned in v. 14. — Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

**v. 25 — The other ends of the chains fastened to the filigree settings on the shoulder-pieces of the ephod at the front.**

The two loose ends of the two braided chains are bound firmly to the gold settings (rosettes, "ouches") located on the shoulder-pieces of the ephod, on the front side. The ephod's shoulder-pieces thus supported the breastpiece from above. — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm ; Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

**v. 26 — Two more gold rings on the lower corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod.**

These are a second pair of rings, placed on the two lower corners of the breastpiece, "in the border thereof" — at the extreme edge. They are positioned on the inner side, i.e., the side facing the ephod. — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm ; Pulpit, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/28-23.htm

**v. 27 — Two additional gold rings attached to the ephod itself, at the bottom of the shoulder-pieces, near the seam above the woven waistband.**

Two gold rings were sewn onto the ephod, low down and in front, so as to appear just above the "curious girdle" (woven waistband) of the ephod. — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

Keil & Delitzsch explain these rings were put "upon the shoulder-pieces of the ephod underneath, toward the fore-part thereof, near the joining above the girdle of it." — Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

**v. 28 — The breastpiece rings tied to the ephod rings with a blue cord, so the breastpiece sits above the waistband and does not swing out.**

The lower rings of the breastpiece were laced to the lower rings of the ephod by a "lace of blue" (a blue cord or ribbon). This secured the breastpiece firmly against the ephod, positioned above the waistband without covering it or swinging loose. — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm ; Pulpit, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/28-23.htm

The Pulpit Commentary summarizes verses 23–28: the breastpiece had four rings — two at the upper corners for the gold chains connecting to the shoulder-settings, and two at the lower corners laced with blue cord to rings on the ephod. By these four fastenings the breastpiece was securely attached and "could not readily get loose from it." — Pulpit, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/28-23.htm

---

## Verse 29: Aaron Bears Israel's Names Over His Heart

**v. 29 — Whenever Aaron enters the Holy Place, he shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment, as a continual reminder before the LORD.**

David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that bearing the names "over his heart" shows the priest must not only work for the people (bearing them on his shoulders) but must also love them. "It isn't enough for a priest to have a heart for God. He must also have a heart for the people." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Keil & Delitzsch explain that the heart, in the biblical view, is the centre of the spiritual life — not only of the will and thought but also the seat of feelings and affections. To "bear upon the heart" denotes a "personal intertwining with the life of another," so that the high priest stood in the deepest sympathy with those for whom he interceded. The high priest brought Israel into remembrance before Jehovah "that the Lord might accept His people." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

Dr. Constable notes: "The high priest carried the tribes on his heart (Exodus 28:30) as well as on his shoulders. The heart refers to the seat of feelings and affections in the Old Testament." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

---

## Verse 30: The Urim and Thummim

**v. 30 — Place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece of judgment, so they will be over Aaron's heart whenever he comes before the LORD. Aaron will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD.**

*What they were:* The names mean "Lights" (Urim) and "Perfections" (Thummim). David Guzik notes the best guess is they were a pair of stones, one light and one dark, each indicating a "yes" or "no" from God when the high priest inquired. The breastpiece is called the "breastpiece of judgment" precisely because it held these tools for discerning God's will. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Keil & Delitzsch state that the Urim and Thummim cannot be determined with certainty. The LXX renders them "revelation and truth" (δήλωσις καὶ ἀλήθεια); Symmachus and Theodotion render "illumination and completion" (φωτισμοὶ καὶ τελειώσεις). Keil & Delitzsch conclude they were a medium given by the Lord through which divine illumination was guaranteed when the congregation needed guidance, and that they were bound up with the high priest's official dress — "a pledge that the Lord would maintain the rights of His people, and give them through the high priest the illumination requisite for their protection." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the etymological meaning (Urim from "light," Thummim from "completeness" or "innocence") has led some scholars to surmise the lot may have had a double purpose in trial ordeals: Urim brought guilt to light, Thummim established innocence. The encyclopedia confirms they were material objects small enough to be inserted into the breastpiece "pouch." — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15224a.htm

Dummelow's Commentary says: "In all probability they were two images or jewels, engraved with distinguishing characters, used in casting lots." It notes that 1 Samuel 14:41 in the Greek and Latin versions reads: "If the iniquity be in me or Jonathan my son, give Urim; and if the iniquity be in the people, give Thummim." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-28.html

The Expositor's Bible Commentary says of their nature and the manner in which they became significant, "nothing can be said that is not pure conjecture." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-28.html

Dr. Constable (citing Youngblood) notes: "The word 'Urim' begins with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet and 'Thummim' begins with the last letter, so the lots were probably restricted to giving either positive or negative responses to questions. … 'Urim and Thummim' is best translated into English as 'curses and perfections,' meaning that if 'Urim' dominated when the lots were cast the answer would be no but if 'Thummim' dominated the answer would be yes." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

---

## Verses 31–35: The Robe of the Ephod

**v. 31 — Make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth.**

The robe (me'il) was an upper garment, all of dark-blue purple (hyacinth). It was not a cloak or mantle but a long, closely-fitting coat reaching to the knees, so as to show the tunic underneath. — Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

David Guzik notes: "This was the basic covering of the priest, made of all blue, and seamless." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Keil & Delitzsch say the dark-blue colour indicated "the heavenly origin and character of the office with which the robe was associated." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

**v. 32 — An opening at its top in the centre, with a woven collar like that of a coat of mail, so that it will not tear.**

The opening for the head was in the middle of the robe, with a strong woven hem around it — "weavers' work" — like the opening of a linen coat of mail (a linen habergeon, such as worn in Egypt). This strong binding prevented tearing when the robe was put on. The robe was therefore woven in one piece, not sewn from multiple parts. — Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

**v. 33 — Pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn around the lower hem, with gold bells between them.**

**v. 34 — Alternating gold bells and pomegranates around the lower hem of the robe.**

The pomegranates were made of twisted yarn in the three colours; the bells were of pure gold. They alternated: a golden bell, then a pomegranate, all around the hem. — Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

David Guzik cites Cole: "The pomegranates (symbols of fruitfulness) were either hanging as 'bobbles' between the bells, or else embroidered on the fabric." G. Campbell Morgan adds: "The alternating bell and pomegranate on the skirts of the priest's robe were typical of his obligation to testimony and fruit bearing." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Keil & Delitzsch develop a major symbolic interpretation: The pomegranates — with their pleasant odour, sweet juice, and rich kernel — were symbols of the word and testimony of God as a sweet spiritual food that enlivens the soul (comparing Proverbs 25:11; Psalm 19:8; 119:25, 43, 50). The bells were symbols of the sounding or proclamation of that word. Thus the high priest, through this robe, was "the recipient and medium of the word and testimony which came down from heaven." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

Dr. Constable records that some interpreters see pomegranates and bells as representing fruitfulness and joy; others see them as representing the fruits and gifts of God's Spirit (citing Sailhamer). He also notes a popular Jewish interpretation that a rope was tied to the high priest's ankle — if the bells stopped ringing, the people would know he had died and could pull him out. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

**v. 35 — Aaron must wear the robe whenever he ministers; its sound will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD, so that he will not die.**

Ellicott explains: "The great object of the bells was to make known to the people, by a sensible manifestation, every movement of their representative, every act that he performed on their behalf. The bells enabled them to follow in their thoughts the entire service that he was engaged in, to join their prayers and praises with his, and offer to God a common worship. So important was this union of priest and people in the worship of God regarded, that death was denounced on the high priest who should minister in the sanctuary without this essential garment." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

David Guzik offers the complementary view: if the high priest were to die, the bells would stop ringing and he could be pulled out of the Most Holy Place. The sound also reminded the priest of the solemn, life-or-death stakes of his work. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Keil & Delitzsch critique the view that the bells enabled the congregation to follow the priest's movements, arguing this would make the priest's life depend on the people's prayers. They insist the bells signified the high priest as bearer of the divine word: "he could only do so when wearing the robe of the word of God, as the bearer of the divine testimony, upon which the covenant fellowship with the Lord was founded." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

---

## Verses 36–38: The Gold Plate — "HOLY TO THE LORD"

**v. 36 — Make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD.**

The gold plate (tsits) was a pure gold plaque engraved like a signet-seal with the words "Holiness to Jehovah." — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

**v. 37 — Fasten it with a blue cord to mount it on the front of the turban.**

The plate was attached by a blue ribbon or "lace" to the front of the turban (mitre), which was made of fine white linen wound in several thick folds. — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

David Guzik notes: "The turban (literally something wound around: the Talmud tells us that eight yards of material were used)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

**v. 38 — It will be on Aaron's forehead, so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate, so that they may be acceptable before the LORD.**

David Guzik explains: Even the gifts and sacrifices the priests brought before the Lord were touched with iniquity. Yet when God's appointed priest brought them in God's appointed way, God accepted them. The inscription indicated "first and foremost the high priest was the servant of God, not man." He cites Trapp: "Hence it was not lawful for the high priest, say the Jews, to put off his bonnet to whomsoever he met." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Keil & Delitzsch comment: "Through this inscription, which was fastened upon his head-dress of brilliant white, the earthly reflection of holiness, he was crowned as the sanctified of the Lord (Psalm 106:16), and endowed with the power to exterminate the sin which clung to the holy offerings of the people on account of the unholiness of their nature, so that the gifts of the nation became well-pleasing to the Lord." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

Dr. Constable cites Durham: "'Set apart for Yahweh' refers not alone, indeed not even primarily to 'Aaron' … It is Israel that is 'set apart for Yahweh,' Aaron of course among Israel and representing Israel." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

---

## Verse 39: The Tunic, Turban, and Sash

**v. 39 — Weave the tunic with fine linen, make the turban of fine linen, and fashion an embroidered sash.**

These were the inner garments. Ellicott lists them as: linen drawers (vv. 42–43), a linen tunic or shirt "woven in a peculiar way," and a girdle of many colours ornamented with embroidery to confine the tunic. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

These items completed the high priest's wardrobe: the tunic was an undergarment, the turban covered his head, and the sash served as a belt. — Dr. Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

---

## Verses 40–41: Garments for Aaron's Sons — Ordination

**v. 40 — Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron's sons, to give them glory and splendor.**

The ordinary priests wore simpler garments than the high priest: linen tunics (coats), girdles (sashes), and caps (bonnets, headbands). — Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

Ellicott observes it is "certainly remarkable that so plain a dress … — a white tunic, a girdle, which may or may not have been embroidered, and a plain white close-fitting cap — should be regarded as sufficing 'for glory and for beauty.'" Yet he notes that white robes are "in Scripture constantly represented as eminently glorious" (Daniel 7:9; Mark 9:3; Revelation 4:4; 7:9–14 etc.). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

Gill notes the bonnets were coverings for the head, of the same kind as the mitre of the high priest and of the same length, but differed in the manner of wrapping the linen. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-28.html

David Guzik notes: the regular priests' garments were simple clothes of fine linen — special, "but not much compared to the glory and beauty of the High Priest's garments," because they had "a far lesser office." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

**v. 41 — After putting these garments on Aaron and his sons, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests.**

David Guzik (citing G. Campbell Morgan) explains the three terms: (1) *Anoint* — the application of sacred oil, representing the filling and continual reliance upon the power of the Holy Spirit. (2) *Consecrate* — literally "the filling of the open hand," signifying the perfect equipment for ministry. (3) *Sanctify* — literally "to make clean," referring to spiritual and moral separation from all defilement. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Gill notes that the putting on of the garments by Moses under God's authority was "a solemn investiture of them with the priestly office," giving them the right to exercise it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-28.html

---

## Verses 42–43: The Linen Undergarments

**v. 42 — Make linen undergarments to cover their bare flesh, extending from waist to thigh.**

Ellicott renders "linen breeches" as "linen drawers" — reaching from the waist to a little above the knee. They were "the sole garment of many in Egypt, a necessary garment of all." Their object was to cover nakedness. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

Gill says: "great care was taken, in the service of God's house, to preserve decency, prevent immodesty, and to guard against laughter and levity." He cites Maimonides that they had strings but no opening before or behind, drawn up like a purse — "somewhat like our sailors' trousers." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-28.html

David Guzik notes this was probably a reaction to the nakedness of pagan priests in their rituals. He cites Clarke: "This command had in view the necessity of purity and decency … in opposition to the shocking indecency of the pagan worship in general, in which the priests often ministered naked, as in the sacrifices to Bacchus." Guzik adds: "Also, the trousers were to be made of cool linen, instead of warm wool. God doesn't want His servants to sweat." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

Dr. Constable, citing Sailhamer, notes: "This prescription for undergarments alludes to and reminds one of the clothing which God made for Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden to cover their nakedness (Genesis 3:21)." He also observes that all the priests ministered barefoot out of reverence for the holiness of God (cf. Exodus 3:5; Joshua 5:15). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

**v. 43 — Aaron and his sons must wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister in the Holy Place, so that they will not incur guilt and die. This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants.**

Ellicott explains that "the holy place" here means the court of the tabernacle, within which the altar stood. "The death penalty is threatened against the sin of ministering without the garments needed for decency, as against the sin of neglecting to wear the robe of the ephod (v. 35). In both cases a Divine vengeance, rather than a legal punishment, is probably intended." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm

Gill states that according to Maimonides, a high priest without his eight garments or a common priest without his four garments rendered his service "illegal and rejected," and he was "guilty of death by the hand of heaven" — deserving of immediate death from God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-28.html

The NET Bible note (cited by Dr. Constable) summarizes the overall point: "Those whom God selects to minister to the congregation through intercessory prayer, divine counsel, and sacrificial worship, must always represent the holiness of Yahweh in their activities and demeanor." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Distinctives Found

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the Urim and Thummim as tools for practical discernment better than "feelings or appearances," and repeatedly draws a sharp contrast between the Old Testament high priest's glory and Christ's humiliation — "Jesus accomplished His priestly work stripped, mocked, and wearing a crown of thorns." Also notes the pomegranates and bells as symbols of "testimony and fruit bearing" (citing Morgan). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/

**Lutheran / Conservative Protestant (Keil & Delitzsch):** Stresses the robe and its pendants as symbols of the Word of God — the pomegranates as the nourishing Word, the bells as its proclamation. Rejects the "rope around the ankle" tradition and the idea that the bells enabled the congregation to follow the priest (arguing this would subject the priest's life to the people's will). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-28.html

**Catholic (Haydock / Catholic Encyclopedia):** The Vulgate and Douay-Rheims render the breastpiece as the "rational" (rationale). The Catholic Encyclopedia treats the Urim and Thummim as "the sacred lot" — a material object used to seek manifestations of the Divine will alongside dreams and prophecy. Haydock's commentary notes that the Urim and Thummim "were not in the second temple" (citing 1 Esdras 2:63), so the oracle was lost after the Babylonian exile. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15224a.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/exodus-28.html

**Baptist / Reformed (Gill):** Emphasises the typological dimension: the ephod as emblematic of Christ's human nature, the breastpiece as emblematic of the church borne on Christ's heart, the girdle as emblematic of Christ's faithfulness and integrity (righteousness being the girdle of His loins, faithfulness the girdle of His reins). The common priests' linen garments signify purity of doctrine and life. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-28.html
